15686.subject: Government
15686.question_text: A Nigeria citizen can only be deprived of his citizenship if he is
15686.explanation:
The 1999 Constitution of Nigeria (Section 30) states that citizenship may be deprived only for those who acquired it by registration or naturalisation (not by birth). The grounds include:

  • If the person is convicted by a court of law for a criminal offence punishable by imprisonment of three years or more, within seven years of becoming a citizen.

  • If the person obtained citizenship by fraud or false representation.

  • If the person shows disloyalty to Nigeria or acts contrary to its interests.

The Constitution does not mention death sentences as a ground for deprivation. Marriage has no effect on Nigerian citizenship. Nigerians by birth can hold dual citizenship. Only naturalised/registered citizens face restrictions. Being an armed robber alone does not automatically remove citizenship; only a court conviction for a serious crime does.

options.text: convicted by a court of law

15720.subject: Government
15720.question_text: Which of the following is not an accepted way of resolving international conflict?
15720.explanation:
Accepted ways of resolving international conflict aim to reduce tension and restore order through negotiation, influence or controlled force. Diplomacy involves negotiation and dialogue between countries to resolve disputes peacefully. This is an accepted and widely used method.

Propaganda, though controversial, can be used to influence public opinion or sway international perspectives without direct violence. Non-military use of force includes sanctions, blockades or cyber tactics that stop short of war. It can also be used as a coercive strategy short of war.

Military force (war), although destructive, is still an accepted (though last-resort) method of resolving some international conflicts in extreme cases, especially under the just war theory or self-defence under international law.

However, Nuclear war is not an accepted method because of its catastrophic humanitarian and environmental consequences. The use of nuclear weapons is widely condemned under international norms, and global treaties like the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) aim to prevent it. It is seen as unacceptable and disproportionate in conflict resolution.

15722.subject: Government
15722.question_text: The membership of the Council of States in Nigeria is made up of
15722.explanation:
The Council of State in Nigeria is composed of key figures, including all the state governors, the President (as Chairman), the Vice President (as Deputy Chairman), all former Presidents and Heads of State, all former Chief Justices of Nigeria, the President of the Senate, the Speaker of the House of Representatives, and the Attorney General of the Federation. 

The Council of State in Nigeria serves as an advisory body to the President. Its duties include:

  1. Advising the President on matters such as:

    • National population census and the maintenance of related records.

    • The exercise of the prerogative of mercy.

    • Awarding national honours.

    • Appointments to key bodies like the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), the National Judicial Council (NJC), and the National Population Commission (NPC).

  2. Providing counsel on maintaining public order within the federation or any part of it.

  3. Offering advice on other matters as directed by the President.

options.text: the leader of state and the traditional chiefs
the state governors and the head of state

15734.explanation:
The Armed Forces Ruling Council (AFRC) was established in 1985 after General Ibrahim Badamasi Babangida overthrew General Muhammadu Buhari in a palace coup.

  • Under General Ironsi (1966) → The governing body was the Supreme Military Council.

  • Under General Gowon (1966–1975) → He ruled mainly through the Supreme Military Council.

  • Under General Obasanjo (1976–1979) → Also operated with the Supreme Military Council before handing over to civilians in 1979.

  • Under General Buhari (1983–1985) → The ruling body was the Supreme Military Council too.

  • But under General Babangida (1985–1993) → He replaced the Supreme Military Council with the Armed Forces Ruling Council (AFRC), which became the highest decision-making body during his regime.

15742.subject: Government
15742.question_text: Residual powers under the Nigerian Independence Constitution were the powers exercised by
15742.explanation:
Under the Nigerian Independence Constitution of 1960, powers were divided between the Federal Government and the Regional Governments through three legislative lists:

  1. Exclusive Legislative List – powers exercised only by the Federal Government (e.g. defence, foreign affairs, currency).

  2. Concurrent Legislative List – powers exercised by both Federal and Regional Governments (e.g. education, health, trade).

  3. Residual Powers – powers not listed in either the Exclusive or Concurrent Lists.

Who controlled the residual powers?

Residual powers were left to the Regional Governments — meaning any matter not assigned to the federal or concurrent lists automatically became the responsibility of the regions.

options.text: both the Federal and Regional Governments
both the Local and regional Govenments

15777.subject: Government
15777.question_text: Which of the following is not an aim of the Organization of African Unity (OAU)?
15777.explanation:
The Organization of African Unity (OAU), founded in 1963, had the following main aims:

  1. Promote unity and solidarity among African states

  2. Coordinate and intensify cooperation for a better life for African people

  3. Defend the sovereignty, territorial integrity, and independence of African states

  4. Eradicate colonialism and all forms of foreign domination

As for Option E, enthronement of democratic governments, this was not an explicit founding aim of the OAU. The OAU’s principle was non-interference in the internal affairs of member states, which meant it did not enforce democracy. That emphasis only came later with the African Union (AU), its successor.

Instead of defiance, the OAU promoted defense of sovereignty.
